Agriculture — Key Details (Wikipedia Summary)
Definition: Agriculture is the practice of cultivating soil, planting, raising, and harvesting food and non-food crops, plus livestock production. Broad definitions add forestry and aquaculture. The word comes from Latin ager (field) + cultura (cultivation).
HISTORY
- Grains gathered by humans from at least 105,000 years ago; planting began around 11,500 years ago.
- Domestication: sheep, goats, pigs, cattle around 10,000 years ago; agriculture arose

stication: sheep, goats, pigs, cattle around 10,000 years ago; agriculture arose independently in at least 11 regions of the world.
- Early centers: rice in China (~5700 BC), wheat/barley in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and the Indus Valley; maize from teosinte in Mesoamerica; potato in the Andes.
- Key advances: Sumerian irrigation (~8000 BC), Egyptian Nile farming, Chinese granaries and ploughs, the Arab Agricultural Revolution, the Columbian Exchange (1492), and the British Agricultural Revolution (17

tion, the Columbian Exchange (1492), and the British Agricultural Revolution (17th century).
- 20th century: industrial agriculture based on large-scale monocultures came to dominate output; the Haber-Bosch process enabled synthetic fertilizer and huge yield gains.
FARM TYPES
- Pastoralism: herding livestock, moved in search of pasture (arid regions).
- Shifting cultivation: clear/burn forest, farm a few years, then move on.
- Subsistence farming: grown for family/local needs (~2.5 billion farme

move on.
- Subsistence farming: grown for family/local needs (~2.5 billion farmers, ~60% of arable land).
- Intensive farming: maximize output with low fallow and high inputs (developed countries).
FARM SIZES AND WORKFORCE
- Small farms (2 hectares or less) are 5 of every 6 farms worldwide but hold only ~12% of farmland; farms over 50 ha are just 1% of farms yet cover over 70% of farmland. Small farms still produce about one-third of the world's food.
- Employment: 916 million people (2023), ~27

bout one-third of the world's food.
- Employment: 916 million people (2023), ~27% of the global workforce (40% in 2000). Agriculture is about 4% of global GDP.
- Women are ~47% of the agricultural workforce in sub-Saharan Africa and earn ~18% less than men in farm wages.
PRODUCTION
- Global output: about 11 billion tonnes of food, 32 million tonnes of natural fibres, 4 billion cubic metres of wood per year; ~14% of food is lost before retail.
- Top crops (million tonnes): sugarcane 1,794; maize

ood is lost before retail.
- Top crops (million tonnes): sugarcane 1,794; maize 883; rice 722; wheat 704; potatoes 374.
- Largest producers by output: China, India, EU, USA, Brazil.
- Livestock systems: grassland-based, mixed, and landless (factory farming — 75% of future growth expected in confined operations).
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
- Agriculture covers 4.8 billion hectares — one-third of Earth's land surface — the biggest human impact on land and water of any sector.
- Uses ~70% of global fresh

iggest human impact on land and water of any sector.
- Uses ~70% of global freshwater withdrawals; 64% of agricultural land is at risk of pesticide pollution.
- Contributes 13-21% of global greenhouse gas emissions; livestock alone is about 18% (CO2-eq), plus 37% of methane and 65% of ammonia.
- Drives ~90% of deforestation; ~40% of agricultural land is seriously degraded.
- Pesticide use rose 62% (2000-2021); ~3 million pesticide poisonings/year with 220,000 deaths (WHO, 1992).
- Plastic (agrip

lion pesticide poisonings/year with 220,000 deaths (WHO, 1992).
- Plastic (agriplastic films, mulch) adds major soil microplastic contamination (50-260 kg/ha in old mulch areas).
CLIMATE CHANGE
- Warming has already slowed agricultural productivity growth over the past 50 years in mid/low latitudes (IPCC 2022).
- At just 1.5 C warming, large crop areas enter danger zones — near 50% of cropland in the Middle East/North Africa.
- FAO estimates agriculture must produce ~50% more food, feed and fibr

h Africa.
- FAO estimates agriculture must produce ~50% more food, feed and fibre by 2050 compared with 2012.
- Disasters cost agriculture US$3.26 trillion (1991-2023), about US$99 billion per year.
BIOTECHNOLOGY AND SAFETY
- GMO crops (herbicide-tolerant, insect-resistant/Bt) are widely used; some countries ban them; EU labelling since 1997, US labelling since 2022.
- Plant breeding (Mendel-based genetics, Green Revolution hybrids) lifted wheat yields from under 1 t/ha (1900) to over 2.5 t/ha (

olution hybrids) lifted wheat yields from under 1 t/ha (1900) to over 2.5 t/ha (1990); US maize from ~2.5 to ~9.4 t/ha.
- Safety: agriculture is among the most hazardous industries — at least 170,000 work deaths/year (ILO), twice the average of other jobs; tractor rollovers are a leading killer.
SUSTAINABILITY AND POLICY
- Movements: organic (EU certified since 1991), regenerative, and sustainable agriculture; conservation tillage, agroforestry, and precision/robotic automation improve efficienc

vation tillage, agroforestry, and precision/robotic automation improve efficiency.
- Global producer support is about US$540 billion/year (15% of production value), often inefficient and environmentally harmful.
- Future focus: automation with AI/robots, water-efficient precision farming, and closing gender gaps in land, inputs, and technology access.
Source: Wikipedia — Agriculture, page last edited 23 September 2026.
